title: Universal distillation of quantum entanglement
authors: Ryuji Takagi, Kaito Watanabe, Takaya Matsuura, Hayato Arai, Masahito Hayashi
abstract: Distillable entanglement---the maximum rate of Bell states extractable from the given noisy entangled states via local operations and classical communication (LOCC)---has been a central quantity to characterize the operational value of entangled states. However, this operational meaning had been known to be valid only under a crucial assumption: both parties know the description of the input state and can choose the protocol tailored to it, which does not necessarily reflect the natural operational setting. Here, we show that the distillable entanglement is the fundamental operational quantity even without this assumption. We present a universal LOCC protocol---whose description does not depend on the input state and thus works universally for any input---that achieves the distillable entanglement of an arbitrary unknown input state. Our result therefore lifts the distillable entanglement to a robust notion of an operationally meaningful quantity and clarifies that input-state knowledge is not necessary to achieve the optimal rate of entanglement distillation. Our protocol is based on state merging for compound states, together with the uniform convergence property of the finite-block quantity toward distillable entanglement.
summary: This work addresses the limitation of entanglement distillation theory that previously required knowing the exact input state. The authors introduce a universal protocol that achieves the maximum distillable entanglement rate using only local operations and classical communication, making $E_d$ a robust measure for unknown quantum states.
main_problem: To establish distillable entanglement as a fundamental operational quantity even when the parties do not know the exact description of the input quantum state (state-agnostic distillation).
main_result: The authors prove that a universal LOCC protocol exists that achieves the distillable entanglement rate for any unknown input state, confirming its operational significance.
method: The protocol is constructed using state merging techniques applied to multiple copies of the state, combined with the uniform convergence property of finite-block estimates.
model_or_system: The study concerns bipartite quantum states $\rho_{AB}$ acting on a tensor product Hilbert space, characterizing the rate of extracting Bell states.
key_observables: Distillable Entanglement ($E_d$), Coherent Information ($I_c$), and the asymptotic rate of entanglement extraction.
important_parameters: The number of copies ($n$), the estimation error ($\epsilon_n$), and the noise strength parameter ($\xi_k$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the ability to perform local informationally complete measurements and the convergence of finite-block estimates to the true distillable entanglement.
paper_structure: The paper first reviews the standard state-aware definition of $E_d$, then introduces the universal protocol based on state merging and local estimation, culminating in the proof that the rate converges to $E_d(ho_{AB})$ regardless of prior state knowledge.
why_interesting: It provides a robust, operational definition for entanglement distillation that holds even in realistic scenarios where the quantum state is unknown, which is crucial for quantum communication protocols.
